title: Characterizing Photonic Partial Distinguishability Through Gram Matrix Tomography
authors: Marcin Kotowski, Marco Robbio, Oliver Reardon-Smith, Benoit Seron, Leonardo Novo, Ernesto F. Galvão, Michał Oszmaniec
abstract: Partial distinguishability affects multiphoton interference, which is central to large-scale photonic experiments such as Boson Sampling and to applications of multiphoton states across quantum technologies. Characterizing the internal degrees of freedom responsible for this behavior is challenging: in many scenarios they cannot be accessed directly and even their dimension or physical nature may be unknown \emph{a priori}. Here we introduce Gram-matrix tomography for independently prepared photons with pure or nearly pure internal states. For pure states, the Gram matrix contains all information required to predict the statistics of experiments that are insensitive to the internal degrees of freedom. We reconstruct this matrix, up to physically irrelevant phase choices, from a quadratic number of measurable Bargmann invariants (quantities encoding overlap magnitudes and collective phases). We access these quantities using two complementary approaches: targeted Fourier interferometers and two- and three-body photon-number correlations measured in a single random interferometer. We derive explicit error bounds that control the total-variation distance between predicted and actual outcome distributions for any subsequent experiment that is insensitive to the internal states. These guarantees account for finite sampling and deviations from purity. Crucially, the total sample complexity of the protocol is independent of the internal Hilbert-space dimension and polynomial under mild assumptions on overlaps of internal states. Our protocol uses standard interferometric measurements and turns them into a robust and operationally grounded characterization of partially distinguishable photons.
summary: This paper introduces Gram-matrix tomography to characterize photonic partial distinguishability, a key hurdle for large-scale quantum experiments. By measuring specific multi-photon correlation invariants, the authors reconstruct the Gram matrix, which fully describes the interference statistics. The protocol offers robust, operationally guaranteed bounds on the fidelity of the external state, independent of the internal dimension.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of characterizing photonic partial distinguishability, which degrades multiphoton interference crucial for quantum technologies like Boson Sampling.
main_result: They develop a tomography protocol to reconstruct the Gram matrix from measurable Bargmann invariants, providing operational guarantees on the fidelity of the external state.
method: The core method is Gram-matrix tomography, utilizing two complementary measurement protocols—targeted Fourier interferometers and single random interferometers—to estimate necessary invariants.
model_or_system: The system involves photons whose internal degrees of freedom (e.g., polarization, frequency) are partially distinguishable, leading to an external state $\Omega_{	ext{ext}}(ho)$ that governs interference statistics.

important_parameters: The total sample complexity is shown to be independent of the internal Hilbert-space dimension and polynomial in the number of photons ($n$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the state is either pure or a product state close to pure, and the reconstruction relies on the invertibility of associated linear systems.

paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the problem (partial distinguishability) to introducing the Gram matrix as the key object. It then details two measurement protocols to estimate the necessary Bargmann invariants, culminating in theorems that provide operational error bounds (Total-Variation distance) for the reconstructed external state.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous, experimentally grounded framework for characterizing fundamental resource limitations (distinguishability) in photonic quantum computation, directly impacting the feasibility of large-scale quantum optical experiments.
